summaries.gardner: Santander does not fit the Rule Breaker profile. It is a 169-year-old universal bank in a mature industry with no top-dog position in an emerging market. Its only Gardner-style traits are strong recent price momentum (the ADR is up about 36% over 52 weeks) and a globally recognised brand.
summaries.buffett: Santander is an understandable deposit-funded franchise that earned a record EUR 14,101M in 2025 with a 17.1% RoTE, and it is buying back shares heavily. Its record is uneven, though: a EUR 8,771M loss in 2020 after goodwill write-downs, a cancelled 2019 final dividend, and earnings tied to emerging markets and interest rates. Buffett usually prefers steadier, less leveraged compounders.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the scale, low-cost deposits and disciplined cost base (41.2% efficiency ratio in 2025). He would worry, though, about the bank's leverage, its exposure to Brazil and Argentina, and doing two large acquisitions (TSB, Webster) at once. It is a fair business at a fair price rather than a great business.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms Santander is a stalwart with a mild turnaround element: profit rose from EUR 9,605M in 2022 to EUR 14,101M in 2025, and diluted EPS from EUR 0.537 to EUR 0.900. At about 11x trailing earnings, its P/E is close to its recent EPS growth, which Lynch would see as reasonable but not a bargain.
summaries.fisher: Fisher would credit management's push to put the group on shared global platforms (ONE Transformation, Openbank, Getnet) and its falling cost per customer. He would doubt that a bank has the kind of product pipeline, R&D or sales edge his 15 points look for, so the fit is partial.
summaries.graham: Santander passes Graham's size test and trades at about 11x trailing earnings, but it fails his record tests: it lost money in 2020, cancelled its 2019 final dividend, and at about 2.05x tangible book its P/E times P/B is well above 22.5.
summaries.thiel: Santander is not a Zero-to-One company: it has no ten-times-better technology and no monopoly in a new market, and it competes in crowded, regulated banking markets. Its strengths are distribution and scale, which Thiel counts but which do not make a monopoly business.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner would note the 'get fit' discipline (costs flat in H1 2026, a 42.8% efficiency ratio, EUR 10bn-plus of buybacks for 2025-26) and rising returns. But Santander does not ride the AI or compute-platform shifts he favours, so it fits only his valuation and efficiency lens.
summaries.druckenmiller: The setup has some Druckenmiller-style positives: earnings are accelerating (H1 2026 attributable profit up 31%), and the 2026-2028 plan targets more than EUR 20bn of profit. Against that, falling European rates and emerging-market currency risk mean the macro backdrop is not clearly favourable, so it is a cyclical value idea rather than a high-conviction liquidity trade.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids banks because they rely on leverage and do not earn high returns on unleveraged capital. Santander's 17.1% RoTE is built on a EUR 1.95 trillion balance sheet with about 14.0% CET1 capital, so it fails his 'good company' test.
summaries.greenblatt: The Magic Formula's return on capital and earnings yield based on enterprise value do not apply to banks, which Greenblatt excludes. On simple earnings yield (about 9% at 11x trailing earnings) the stock looks cheap, but the screen itself does not fit.
summaries.akre: On Akre's three-legged stool: the business earns decent but not exceptional returns (RoTE of 17.1%), management is capable with a family chair, and reinvestment goes largely into acquisitions and buybacks rather than high-return organic compounding. It is only a partial fit.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for low-risk, high-uncertainty bets at deep discounts. Santander at about 2x tangible book after a strong rerating no longer offers that discount, and bank leverage means the downside is not clearly limited.
summaries.wood: Santander is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's sense: it is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomics. Its digital efforts (Openbank, Gravity cloud core banking, Getnet) defend an incumbent position rather than open up exponential new markets.
summaries.ackman: Ackman wants simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry and limited outside risks. Santander is simple to describe and has some barriers, but its results depend on interest rates, credit cycles and Latin American economies, so it is not his kind of investment.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economies-shared model fits only partly. Santander's cost per active customer fell 5% to EUR 253, but most of those savings go to shareholders through buybacks rather than to customers through clearly lower prices, and its 10-20-year position is not obviously stronger.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed companies in huge new markets with breakthrough technology. Santander serves a huge but mature market with an incumbent business model, so it is not the kind of opportunity Sequoia looks for.
summaries.nash: Nash's process would screen Santander out early. It is a leveraged incumbent rather than a company built for a secular trend, statutory revenue grew only 0.5% in 2025, and the debt-versus-cash and banker-lending tests fail because it is a bank. The valuation (about 11x forward earnings) is reasonable, but it misses most of his quality filters.

momentum.evidence: The NYSE ADR closed at $13.30 on Oct 16, 2026, up 36.1% over one year and 10.2% year to date, with a 52-week range of $9.62-$15.05.

g4.evidence: The bank is led by experienced managers (CEO Héctor Grisi since 2023 and Executive Chair Ana Botín), but its shareholders are mainly index and institutional funds rather than famous, well-known investors.

g6.evidence: Commentators generally describe Santander as fairly valued or cheap (about 11x trailing earnings), and the consensus rating is Hold with an average price target of $14.79, slightly above the price.

simple.evidence: Taking deposits and lending is simple, but a EUR 1.95 trillion balance sheet in ten countries, with credit, currency and regulatory risks, is hard for a generalist to judge fully.

b2.evidence: Attributable profit rose steadily from EUR 8,124M (2021) to EUR 14,101M (2025), but 2020 brought an EUR 8,771M loss after goodwill write-downs.

integrity.evidence: Disclosure is detailed and capital return is disciplined (about EUR 9bn of buybacks under way toward an at-least-EUR-10bn target for 2025-26), but family-led governance and past conduct issues (such as UK motor-finance commissions) count against it.

b6.evidence: It sold 49% of Santander Bank Polska to Erste for a EUR 1,895M gain, but it also bought TSB and Webster (about $12.3bn) in 2026 to gain scale in the UK and US, which carries some empire-building risk.

roic.evidence: RoTE was 17.1% in 2025 and 15.6% (underlying) in H1 2026, but this is earned on a leveraged balance sheet with total liabilities of EUR 1,838,567M against total equity of EUR 115,898M.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow is not a meaningful measure for a bank, whose cash flows swing with deposits and loans.

b10.evidence: Tangible net asset value per share rose from EUR 4.76 (2023) to EUR 5.76 (2025), but retained earnings over the longer run were offset by the 2020 write-downs and currency losses in Latin America.

safety.evidence: At about 2.05x tangible book (EUR 11.83 per share against TNAV per share of EUR 5.76 at end-2025), there is no clear margin of safety on a conservative value.

fairprice.evidence: About 11.1x trailing EPS (EUR 1.07 including the Poland gain) and 11.4x the FY2026 consensus of EUR 1.04 is reasonable for a bank targeting RoTE above 20% by 2028.

mu5.evidence: Diversification across ten main markets and a 14.0% CET1 ratio make failure unlikely, but bank leverage, emerging-market crises and conduct fines are real ways to lose big.

reinvest.evidence: It can deploy capital into loan growth (up 5% excluding TSB in H1 2026) and acquisitions, but at mid-to-high-teens returns rather than exceptional ones, so it returns about half of profit to shareholders.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart: a large, slow-growing bank whose story is better efficiency, buybacks and a 2028 goal of more than EUR 20bn profit.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 11 is close to the roughly 17% average annual growth in diluted EPS from EUR 0.537 (2022) to EUR 0.900 (2025); forward growth is expected to be slower.

runway.evidence: The US (Webster, Openbank US) and payments offer room to grow, but its core markets grow roughly with nominal GDP, and statutory total income grew only 0.5% in 2025.

ly7.evidence: The company is cutting its share count hard (diluted shares fell from 17,321M in 2021 to 14,976M in 2025), but there is no evidence of significant insider buying.

ly8.evidence: Santander is one of Europe's largest and most widely covered banks.

fi2.evidence: It keeps launching digital offerings (Openbank in the US and Mexico, Getnet platforms, Ebury FX), but these are new channels for existing banking products.

fi3.evidence: Its technology spending on the Gravity cloud core and global platforms cut payments cost per transaction from 2.9 to 1.6 cents and lowered non-commercial staff to 410 per million customers, but banks do not report R&D separately.

fi4.evidence: It added 12 million customers in the year to June 2026, more than 4 million of them through TSB, which shows a strong distribution network but no unusual sales edge over peers.

longterm.evidence: The multi-year ONE Transformation shows a long-term view, but management also commits to a fixed 50% payout and large near-term buybacks.

gr1.evidence: With total assets of EUR 1,954,465M at June 2026 and a market value of about $190bn, it is one of the largest banks in Europe.

ni10.evidence: It reported an attributable loss of EUR 8,771M in 2020.

gr4.evidence: In April 2020 Santander cancelled its EUR 0.13 final dividend for 2019 and its 2020 remuneration policy, following the ECB's recommendation.

eps10.evidence: Attributable profit rose from about EUR 5.97bn in 2015 to EUR 14,101M in 2025, and diluted EPS reached EUR 0.900 in 2025, well over a third higher than the mid-2010s level (exact 2015 EPS not checked).

gr6.evidence: At about EUR 11.83 per share, the price is about 13.1x 2025 diluted EPS of EUR 0.900 and well under 15x average earnings for 2023-2025 (EUR 0.651, 0.768, 0.900).

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 13.1 on 2025 EPS times price to tangible book of about 2.05 gives roughly 27, above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its banking technology is competitive, but not ten times better than BBVA's or Nubank's.

timing.evidence: Profit is near record levels and US expansion is under way, but falling European rates are squeezing net interest income (down from EUR 43,787M in 2024 to EUR 42,348M in 2025).

th3.evidence: It is a 169-year-old incumbent that grew by acquisitions across many large markets, not a business that dominated a small niche first.

team.evidence: Grisi and Botín have delivered record profits and RoTE above 17%, a capable but not world-class team.

th5.evidence: It has a vast distribution network, with 182 million customers, branches across ten main markets, and dealer networks for its auto finance.

durable.evidence: Large regulated banks have lasted for decades, and Santander is a top-three player in most of its markets, but digital banks and payments players are steadily taking fees and young customers.

th7.evidence: Its strategy of scale, efficiency and US expansion is a familiar banking playbook.

trend.evidence: It uses AI and cloud internally but is not a leading beneficiary of any platform shift.

dr1.evidence: H1 2026 attributable profit rose 31% to EUR 8,973M and underlying EPS rose 20%, and management reiterated profit above 2025's EUR 14.1bn.

dr2.evidence: TSB synergies (at least GBP 400M) and Webster's integration could lift US and UK returns by 2027-28, but much of this is already in the 2026-2028 targets.

dr4.evidence: ECB and Bank of England rate cuts squeeze lending margins, while a stable European economy keeps credit costs contained (H1 2026 cost of risk 1.15%).

dr6.evidence: Upcoming drivers include Webster synergies, TSB integration, the EUR 1.8bn H1 2026 buyback and the 2028 targets of more than EUR 20bn profit and RoTE above 20%.

dr7.evidence: Leverage and exposure to Latin America and interest rates make it a poor candidate for a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin does not apply to banks.

fcfyield.evidence: Free cash flow is not meaningful for a bank; on earnings, the FY2026 consensus EPS of EUR 1.04 implies an earnings yield of about 8.8%.

gb2.evidence: Enterprise value is not meaningful for a bank, so this test cannot be applied.

pa2.evidence: The business is near record profitability, not in a temporary setback.

pa4.evidence: A 14.0% CET1 ratio and diversification limit the risk of permanent loss, but bank leverage and emerging-market exposure mean it is not small.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Payments cost per transaction fell to 1.6 cents from 2.9 as Getnet volumes grew to 16.6bn transactions, but this is a small part of the group.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several of ARK's innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market of banking in Europe and the Americas will not grow many times over in five years.

ac3.evidence: Results depend heavily on interest rates, credit cycles and currencies, especially the Brazilian real, Mexican peso and Argentine peso.

ns1.evidence: Cost per active customer fell 5% to EUR 253 and Openbank offers competitive digital rates, but most scale savings go to shareholders.

ns4.evidence: The added US scale (Webster) and UK scale (TSB) should strengthen its position, but digital competition makes a clearly stronger position in 10-20 years uncertain.

va2.evidence: It meets a large basic need for savings, payments and credit, including for underbanked people in Latin America, but these needs are well served by many banks.

tn1.evidence: It is a traditional bank adding digital tools, not a company built for a secular trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees it as a large diversified bank, which is what it is becoming; there is no hidden transformation.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap Spanish bank, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable (EUR 14,101M in 2025) and revenue rose in each recent year (EUR 58,380M to 58,670M in 2025 on the restated basis), but debt instruments of EUR 348,067M exceed cash of EUR 138,008M, as is normal for a bank.

tn5.evidence: Debt instruments issued (EUR 348,067M at June 2026) exceed cash and central-bank balances (EUR 138,008M), and free cash flow is not meaningful for a bank.

tn6.evidence: Statutory total income grew 0.5% in 2025 and 6.4% in H1 2026, below 10%.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of about 0.5-6% plus a free-cash-flow margin that cannot be measured meaningfully does not plausibly reach 40.

tn8.evidence: In H1 2026 total income rose 6% while total costs were flat at EUR 13,211M, and in 2025 total income rose while operating expenses fell from EUR 25,149M to EUR 24,711M.

tn9.evidence: It fails the more-debt-than-cash test, and revenue growth was below 10% (0.5% in 2025), though its operating margin (profit before tax of 31.8% of total income) and age pass.

tn10.evidence: UK motor-finance commission redress, and regulatory approvals and capital rules in several countries, remain live risks, though none threatens the group.

tn11.evidence: It provides savings, payments and credit that help households and businesses in Europe and the Americas manage and grow money, charging interest margins and fees; customers choose it for reach and convenience.

tn13.evidence: Estimated total 65: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 10, short interest 10 (assumed low, not checked), institutional ownership 5 (not checked), revenue vs expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 10 (judged from the ADR's large rerating), moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 0, culture and mission 5, talent 0.

tn14.evidence: Revenue and margins rose, but 2020 was a loss year, debt has exceeded cash every year, and free cash flow is not meaningful for a bank.

tn15.evidence: Total liabilities of EUR 1,838,567M are about 15.9x total equity of EUR 115,898M at June 2026, far above the 4x limit, as for any bank.

tn18.evidence: Grisi has delivered record profit and better efficiency since January 2023, but he has under four years as CEO, is not a founder, and has no record of open-market share purchases that we could find.

tn20.evidence: Recent results such as H1 2026 (profit up 31%, underlying up 15%) were received as solid, but a consistent beat record against consensus was not verified.

tn21.evidence: There is no clown CEO and no accounting suspicion, but the TSB and Webster deals within months of each other look like an acquisition burst, and statutory net interest income margins declined in 2025.

tn22.evidence: It has large revenue (EUR 58,670M in 2025), strong profits, and buys back shares rather than issuing them, apart from ADSs issued for Webster.

tn24.evidence: At about 11x forward earnings, the price implies little growth, below the roughly 17% annual diluted EPS growth delivered from 2022 to 2025.

tn25.evidence: Nash's free-cash-flow DCF cannot be applied meaningfully to a bank.

tn26.evidence: At about 11.4x FY2026 consensus EPS of EUR 1.04, it is in line with large European bank peers, but with EPS growth near 10% its PEG is around 1, not clearly below it.
